transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-2027-08-04-sentinel-001 (note: automated link)
Attendees: Maya Patel (AE, Redwood), Liam Ortega (SE, Redwood), Dr. Helen Park (Head of ML, Sentinel), Rajesh Kumar (Infra Lead), Marta Diaz (Security Manager), Aaron Lee (Product)
Agenda: 1) High level workload & isolation needs; 2) Burst/hotpool strategy and economics; 3) Compliance/ops constraints; 4) Next steps / pilot

Summary:
Sentinel Medical is validating options for moving image- and text-based clinical inference from a prototype on-hosted GPUs to a predictable dedicated environment. Key priorities: strict tenant isolation for PHI, predictable tail-latency for short clinical workflows (95th percentile < 300ms for short prompts), and ability to absorb 6-8x daily burst for triage events. They prefer a hybrid approach (private VPC for PHI plus Redwood Dedicated for steady traffic) and are interested in a short pilot to benchmark costs and latencies. Security (KMS, audit logs, SOC2 scope) is a gating item.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and model shapes (token lengths, sequence length for transcripts and notes)
- Steady-state vs peak QPS, burst multipliers, and hotpool (warm pool) pre-warm strategies
- Isolation options: dedicated tenant pools, node-fencing, on-prem/private deployment considerations
- Cost tradeoffs: reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go + fallback options
- Compliance: SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM, audit logs, data residency

Transcript (timestamps roughly every 30-50s):
[00:00:00] Maya Patel: Okay, thanks everyone for joining. Quick intro from me and Liam on the Redwood side, and then we'd love to hear from Helen about the workload.
[00:00:28] Dr. Helen Park: Hi all, thanks, um yes at a high level we're running two streams: one is clinical note summarization and triage text, the other is imaging metadata captioning. The models are a mix — smaller distilled for notes, larger 7B-ish for multi-modal. Latency is critical for triage, like subsecond ideally.
[00:01:05] Liam Ortega: Got it. When you say 7B-ish, are those quantized? And roughly what's your token distribution and typical prompt length?
[00:01:38] Dr. Helen Park: Mostly 8-bit quantized in prod now, but the prototypes are on A100s w/o quant so we can measure. Prompts vary, 40–300 tokens for notes, imaging captions are shorter. Peak tails are the worry — during surges we can see concentrated bursts from batch uploads.
[00:02:12] Rajesh Kumar: To add, our infra currently runs in GCP us-east4. We have a VPC with strict egress rules, and anything dealing with PHI must stay inside a private subnetwork. We need support for customer-managed KMS and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[00:02:45] Maya Patel: Thanks Rajesh, that's helpful. On the dedicated side Redwood can offer isolated GPU pools inside your VPC (Private deployment) or Dedicated with VPC peering and strict tenancy. For PHI-heavy flows many customers pick Private deployment, but Dedicated with pinned nodes and node-fencing also works — tradeoffs are operational overhead vs uptime SLAs.
[00:03:21] Aaron Lee: Can you explain node-fencing vs pool-level isolation? I know the terms but want the operational picture.
[00:03:46] Liam Ortega: Sure. Node-fencing is basically dedicating physical or logical nodes to a single tenant so noisy neighbors can't interfere. Pool-level isolation uses scheduler and quotas to approximate separation but can still share underlying hardware. Node-fencing is stronger for compliance but costs more.
[00:04:18] Marta Diaz: From security we need key separation, HSM-level KMS or customer-managed keys, and immutable audit trails. Also artifact access control — who can pull model weights, etc.
[00:04:50] Maya Patel: Absolutely — Redwood Private supports bring-your-own-KMS and HSM options; for Dedicated we can integrate with customer KMS via peering and offer encrypted at-rest with rotation policies. We'll send the SOC2 and ISO scope docs.
[00:05:18] Dr. Helen Park: One big question is burst handling. We see unpredictable triage spikes during storms or platform incidents when urgent messages flood in. We need a strategy that keeps latency stable without paying for 10x steady state.
[00:05:46] Liam Ortega: Two common patterns: 1) pre-warmed hotpool (warm instances kept with KV caches to serve low-latency bursts), and 2) multi-tier routing that falls back to hosted or lower-cost quantized variants during extreme peaks. Hotpools are faster but you pay for reserved warm capacity.
[00:06:20] Rajesh Kumar: How does KV cache play into this? Our triage requests have a lot of repeated prefixes. If we can cache prefixes we could cut cost significantly.
[00:06:47] Liam Ortega: Exactly — prefix and KV caching can reduce compute by serving repeated contexts from cache. Redwood's runtime supports automatic prefix caching and continuous batching to maximize GPU utilization while hitting latency SLOs.
[00:07:17] Aaron Lee: What's the typical pre-warm size? Like how many tokens or how many nodes should be kept hot for a 6x burst?
[00:07:44] Maya Patel: It depends on model size and request profile. As a rough starting point, customers reserve ~20–30% of expected peak as hotpool for fast reaction, and then rely on autoscale + fallback for the rest. For example, if steady is 50 qps and peak burst 300 qps, you'd size hotpool for 60–90 qps and let autoscale fill in — but autoscale takes minutes depending on node boot times unless you use pre-warmed images.
[00:08:16] Dr. Helen Park: That's useful. Our desired P95 is < 300ms for short prompts — is that realistic with a hotpool on 7B quantized models?
[00:08:45] Liam Ortega: Yes, with pre-warmed KV cache and continuous batching tuned for low-latency you can hit sub-300ms P95 for many 7B models on A100- or similar-class hardware. But tail-latency spikes come from cold starts and long sequence lengths. We recommend mixing pre-warm and fallback quantized variants.
[00:09:12] Rajesh Kumar: On the Dedicated contract side — what's the commit term flexibility? We may not want a multi-year lock for something this experimental.
[00:09:34] Maya Patel: Redwood Dedicated supports monthly and annual reservations. We can do short-term pilots on monthly reserved nodes and then convert to annual when you're comfortable. There is also burst pool options that let you buy burst credits. We'll include pricing scenarios in the calc.
[00:09:58] Marta Diaz: Compliance question — do you produce audit logs at token-level or request-level? We need forensic trails for access and model input/output for a subset of requests.
[00:10:24] Liam Ortega: We emit request-level logs and can persist payloads to customer-managed storage for a configurable retention window. Token-level logging is heavy and typically optional; we can work with you on sampling or selective retention.
[00:10:52] Aaron Lee: For the pilot, we'd like to measure both cost per inference and P95 latency under 1x, 3x, and 6x load.\n[00:11:15] Maya Patel: Perfect — that aligns with our benchmark checklist. Liam will draft a checklist that includes load phases, model versions, quantization configs, and KV cache warm/cold scenarios.
[00:11:40] Dr. Helen Park: One more infra detail — we have a strict egress policy for PHI. Does Redwood Dedicated require outgoing endpoints, or can it be peer-only?
[00:12:03] Liam Ortega: Dedicated can be configured with VPC peering and restricted egress. For Private on-prem deployments we run inside your network so no outbound egress is required. We'll note the difference in the checklist.
[00:12:30] Rajesh Kumar: For encryption key management, is there an option for periodic rotations triggered by our KMS? And can you support split keys?
[00:12:56] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood integrates with customer-managed KMS and supports key rotation policies. Split-key or HSM-backed keys are supported for Private deployments; we'll include the exact integration patterns.
[00:13:20] Marta Diaz: Also, do you allow only RBAC or granular feature flags to prevent model weight downloads? We need strict control on artifact access.
[00:13:48] Liam Ortega: We have RBAC roles at token and model level — you can restrict who can push or download weights. For Private deployments we can further lock down artifact registries behind your auth.
[00:14:10] Aaron Lee: Cost question — if we do hotpool + fallback to hosted for overspill, how do you bill outbound to hosted? Is that charged at a premium?
[00:14:33] Maya Patel: Overspill to hosted is measured as usage on the hosted API rates; there's no extra hidden surcharge, but you may see differences in per-token cost vs. dedicated. We'll model a few scenarios.
[00:14:58] Dr. Helen Park: In terms of success criteria: 1) pilot shows P95 < 300ms for target model on 1x and 3x; 2) cost within 2x of our cost target for steady-state; 3) SOC2 checklist satisfied. If those are met, we'll look at a larger reserved purchase.
[00:15:28] Maya Patel: That's a very clear set of gates, thanks. We'll map them to the benchmark phases.
[00:15:50] Rajesh Kumar: Practical ops question — how do rollouts work for model updates? We need canary and auto-fallback if a version regresses.
[00:16:15] Liam Ortega: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts by percentage and automatic fallback policies if latency or error budgets are breached. You can pin traffic to older model versions per route.
[00:16:38] Aaron Lee: Do you have integration with our existing tracing stack? We use Datadog and Sentry.
[00:16:58] Maya Patel: Yes, we emit tracing hooks and logs that integrate with Datadog, and you can forward errors to Sentry. We'll include config snippets.
[00:17:22] Dr. Helen Park: A question on quantization: How much model quality regression do you typically see moving from float16 to 4-bit quant? We can't sacrifice clinical accuracy.
[00:17:50] Liam Ortega: It varies by model. For many LLMs, 8-bit per-channel quant (or PTQ/QLoRA style approaches) keeps quality close to fp16; 4-bit aggressive quant can introduce regressions. Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles per workload and keeps a regression alert tied to evaluation prompts.
[00:18:22] Maya Patel: We'll include quality baselines in the pilot and make sure you have rollback options.
[00:18:42] Aaron Lee: For the benchmark, can we test both dedicated and private deployments side-by-side?
[00:18:58] Liam Ortega: Yes, typically customers do a split-run: private or dedicated for PHI flows and dedicated-hosted fallback for non-PHI. We can provision both for a short pilot; cost will reflect the duplicated capacity.
[00:19:25] Rajesh Kumar: How quickly can Redwood spin up pre-warmed nodes? I assume image bake + GPU attach takes a few minutes.
[00:19:46] Maya Patel: With dedicated warm pools we keep images and model cache resident so spin-up is fast — often seconds to tens of seconds for an instance to start serving if pre-warmed. Cold node provisioning from scratch is longer.
[00:20:12] Dr. Helen Park: Any limits on model size for pre-warm? We have some larger multi-modal weights.
[00:20:33] Liam Ortega: Limits depend on GPU memory and quantization; very large models may need model sharding across nodes. For most 7–13B models quantized to 8-bit you can pre-warm on single A100-like nodes. We'll check your exact models in the deep-dive.
[00:20:56] Aaron Lee: Talk through failure modes — if hotpool saturates and fallback goes to hosted, what's the expected latency delta and how do we monitor user impact?
[00:21:20] Liam Ortega: Fallback to hosted may increase latency depending on geographic hops and model variant; we recommend synthetic monitoring and user-facing degradations like shorter responses. Redwood Console can alert when fallback engages and show downstream error/latency impact.
[00:21:52] Marta Diaz: For legal, do you support data residency controls? We need EU data to stay in eu-central for certain clients.
[00:22:16] Maya Patel: Yes — region pinning and routing policies let us keep traffic in specified regions. Private deployments obviously inherit your on-prem region.
[00:22:40] Dr. Helen Park: Great. On ops teams, Rajesh and I would run the benchmark; can you share a test harness template?
[00:22:59] Liam Ortega: We'll send a JMeter/Locust harness and a Redwood benchmark checklist.
[00:23:20] Maya Patel: Quick recap of what we said so everyone's aligned: Redwood will send pricing scenarios and burst calculator, SOC2/ISO + KMS notes, benchmark checklist and harness, and propose dates for a 2-week pilot with dedicated pre-warmed nodes. Sentiel — sorry, Sentinel — will share VPC topology and compliance requirements.
[00:23:59] (crosstalk) Dr. Helen Park: Yep, we'll share the topology.
[00:24:15] Aaron Lee: Timeline-wise, when can Redwood start the pilot?
[00:24:33] Maya Patel: If we get approval this week and contracts for a pilot are signed, we can provision by Aug 9 and start benchmarks Aug 10–24.
[00:24:55] Rajesh Kumar: One more on metrics — can Redwood emit cost-per-request in Console? We want to attribute to product features.
[00:25:18] Liam Ortega: Yes, cost breakouts per token and per-route are standard in Redwood Console; you can tag routes to map to features.
[00:25:40] Dr. Helen Park: Any suggestions for initial sizing? We're currently seeing ~120k tokens/day steady across both workloads, 4x midday peaks for several hours.
[00:25:58] Maya Patel: For 120k tokens/day steady, rough compute depends on model and batching. We'll run the numbers in the calculator but I'd expect 1–2 reserved nodes for steady and a small hotpool of 1 node plus autoscale for peaks. We'll provide scenarios.
[00:26:25] Aaron Lee: Ok that gives us confidence. Marta, anything else from security?
[00:26:40] Marta Diaz: Just prefer explicit SLA clauses around data handling. Also will want a white-glove onboarding for the first month.
[00:26:55] Maya Patel: Noted. We'll include onboarding support options.
[00:27:10] (short silence)
[00:27:30] Maya Patel: Alright, last check — does everyone agree on the next steps as Maya summarized?
[00:27:48] Dr. Helen Park: Yes.
[00:27:55] Rajesh Kumar: Yes.
[00:28:02] Aaron Lee: Yep.
[00:28:10] Maya Patel: Great — we'll follow up with the materials and proposed pilot dates. Thanks everyone.
